heroLead: A biogeographer building miniature, museum-inspired habitats from clay, papier-mâché, recycled materials, and carefully posed figurines.
statement: My work blends elements of natural history—the study of living and extinct life on Earth—with model-building techniques like clay work, papier-mâché, painting, and homemade or recycled materials. And of course, animal figurines.

I depict animals, living or extinct, in their natural habitat scenes—akin to the full-sized dioramas you'd see at a natural history museum. I'm trying to make miniature museum exhibits: small enough to live on a shelf, but built with the same care you'd see behind glass at the Field or the Smithsonian.

My hope is that these dioramas inspire people to visit and support their local natural history museums, and to learn a little more about the world we share with everything else that lives, or once lived, on it.
bio: Christopher Kingwill is an emerging artist and biogeographer specializing in natural history. The path started with childhood obsessions—dinosaurs, wildlife figurines, and “little scenes” built on the floor with Legos and Playmobil.

He studied geography and geosciences, focusing on cartographic mapping and natural history through paleontology and biology coursework. A wildlife conservation internship in Ecuador and time interning at natural history museums sharpened the lens.

After graduate school and a move to Lafayette, Louisiana, art and science outreach across Acadiana brought the old scene-making instinct back—with new materials, a deeper toolkit, and a clear purpose.
